paragraphs: The paper tackles the difficulty of assigning probabilities to sequences of words when the number of possible sequences is enormous. Observed sentences cover only a small portion of that space. The proposed approach addresses this problem by learning representations of words together with a probability model that uses those representations.

Each word receives a distributed representation that expresses similarities to other words. These similarities are learned alongside the sequence probabilities, so the representation and the language model develop together. This creates a route for generalization: an unseen sequence can receive high probability when its words resemble those in a sequence the model has encountered.

The authors implement the probability function with neural networks and evaluate the approach on two text corpora. They report a very significant improvement over a state-of-the-art trigram model. The central contribution is a way to share what is learned across related word sequences, using learned word similarity to address the dimensionality problem in language modeling.
neurips-2000-a-neural-probabilistic-lang.tldr: Jointly learning word representations and sequence probabilities enables generalization to unseen sentences and substantially improves on a trigram model in two corpora.

paragraphs: The paper addresses an obstacle to using sum-product message passing in richly connected probabilistic models. Applying this algorithm while ignoring cycles is one way to approximate inference. However, many conditional probability functions, including the sigmoid function, do not allow the algorithm to be applied directly in the form considered here.

Accumulator networks reorganize how a child variable depends on its parents. Their inputs are combined through a Markov chain, or more generally through a tree, to determine the child's probability. This gives the network low local complexity, making direct sum-product updates possible. Its overall complexity can still be exponential, so tractable local computations do not eliminate the difficulty of the global problem.

The authors derive expressions for both inference and learning in these networks. They also report results on the bars problem and on extracting translated, overlapping faces from an image. The contribution is a model structure designed to accommodate local probability propagation, together with applications illustrating its use in recovering overlapping visual components.
neurips-2000-accumulator-networks-suitor.tldr: Accumulator networks combine parent inputs through chains or trees, enabling direct sum-product updates despite potentially exponential global complexity.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an account of object recognition in which a single primary visual pathway can support apparently specialized representations. It challenges theories that explain visual versatility through separate pathways devoted to different object categories. The alternative assumes a loosely modular pathway with memory modules attached at several stages.

Each memory site independently decides an object's identity. A key assumption links confidence to timing: greater confidence produces a faster response. The observer's answer is whichever site's response arrives first. Consequently, different tasks and stimuli can lead different stages of the same pathway to determine the final decision.

This mechanism can make the system appear specialized when studied experimentally, because the winning decision comes from an appropriate level of abstraction. The authors argue that this account can explain the data addressed by competing theories and additional observations, while remaining consistent with clinical and functional-imaging findings. Its significance is a proposed explanation of flexible recognition through distributed memory and decision timing within one pathway.
neurips-2000-adaptive-object-representat.tldr: A visual pathway with competing memory sites could produce apparently specialized recognition through confidence-dependent response times.

paragraphs: The paper develops guarantees about how well a learning algorithm performs beyond its training data by examining its stability. Here, stability means that a small change to the training set produces only a small change in the learned solution. This makes the learner's sensitivity to its examples central to the analysis.

The resulting bounds have a PAC-style form: they provide probabilistic guarantees on generalization error. Their distinctive feature is that they do not depend on a measure of hypothesis-space complexity such as VC dimension. Instead, they depend on properties of how the learning algorithm searches that space. This allows the approach to apply even when the VC dimension is infinite.

The authors show that regularization networks have the stability property needed for their method and derive new generalization bounds for them. The contribution connects a concrete behavior of a training procedure—resistance to small data changes—to guarantees about performance on unseen data, without requiring a finite hypothesis-space complexity measure.
neurips-2000-algorithmic-stability-and-g.tldr: Stability under small training-set changes yields generalization bounds that can apply even when the hypothesis space has infinite VC dimension.

paragraphs: The paper studies how an agent can learn complex tasks through a hierarchy of subtasks. It uses the options framework, in which an action can extend over time and solve an assigned subtask. The agent learns to choose among these temporally extended actions as part of accomplishing its overall objective.

The authors argue that each option should have a state representation suited to its particular subtask. State abstraction controls which distinctions in the state feature space the learner represents. Making this abstraction option-specific allows the representation to reflect the task being performed. They further argue that automating this process is important if hierarchical learning is to scale to larger tasks.

To implement that idea, the paper adapts the U-Tree algorithm to build state representations separately for different options. A simple hierarchical task illustrates the resulting method. The results suggest that automated, option-specific abstraction is a promising way to improve hierarchical learning, with the demonstration supporting that direction rather than establishing effectiveness across larger tasks.
neurips-2000-automated-state-abstraction.tldr: An adapted U-Tree algorithm automatically builds option-specific state representations, with promising results on a simple hierarchical task.

paragraphs: The paper examines how knowledge of video structure can improve the division of a video into shots. It focuses on two structural properties: how long shots last and how much activity they contain. The authors introduce statistical models for these properties so that they can inform decisions about shot boundaries.

These models become part of a Bayesian formulation of shot segmentation. This provides a way to combine evidence about a boundary with prior knowledge of video structure. The authors show that their formulation extends standard thresholding methods in an adaptive, intuitive manner. The decision process therefore incorporates modeled structural information when deciding where one shot ends and another begins.

The reported result is improved segmentation accuracy. The paper also motivates structural modeling as useful for content analysis and for extracting features that support semantic classification. Its demonstrated contribution is the segmentation formulation: shot duration and activity become explicit sources of information for improving the separation of video into meaningful temporal units.
neurips-2000-bayesian-video-shot-segment.tldr: Statistical models of shot duration and activity support a Bayesian extension of threshold-based video segmentation that improves accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper views several unsupervised learning problems as attempts to align two probability distributions. This perspective covers generative models, including Gaussian mixtures and Boltzmann machines, as well as recoding methods such as independent component analysis and projection pursuit. The authors propose an error measure based on samples for training these kinds of models.

The measure avoids having to approximate a probability density function. It can also apply in situations where maximum-likelihood or density-estimation formulations cannot be used, including some nonlinear models or models with intractable posterior distributions. Its purpose is to make distribution matching available when those conventional formulations are difficult to apply.

For an unconstrained model, the authors prove convergence to the correct solution as the number of samples grows without bound. They also prove that the expected solution in the generative setting is the maximum-likelihood solution. Simulations involving linear and nonlinear models on Gaussian-mixture and independent-component problems demonstrate broad applicability. The theoretical claims retain their stated unconstrained-model and asymptotic conditions.
neurips-2000-beyond-maximum-likelihood-a.tldr: A sample-based distribution-matching criterion broadens unsupervised learning beyond tractable density formulations, with theoretical guarantees for unconstrained models.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for training support vector classifiers on large datasets. Its contribution addresses two parts of the training process: the optimization procedure used to solve the classifier and the selection of examples included in a working set. Both choices concern how the training computation is organized.

The optimization procedure uses iterative reweighted least squares. This means that training proceeds through least-squares calculations whose weights change across iterations. Alongside this procedure, the authors introduce a randomized working-set strategy. It draws its examples from the training samples that do not satisfy the stopping criteria, directing selection toward samples for which the relevant conditions remain unmet.

Computer experiments on well-known datasets support the validity of both proposals. The abstract presents these experiments as evidence for the optimization procedure and the sample-selection strategy. The approach matters because it treats large-scale support vector training as a combination of numerical optimization and selective attention to training examples, with an explicit rule connecting the working set to stopping conditions.
neurips-2000-fast-training-of-support-ve.tldr: The proposed support vector training method combines iterative reweighted least squares with randomized selection among samples that fail stopping criteria.

paragraphs: Belief propagation passes messages through a probabilistic network to estimate quantities such as marginal probabilities. Although developed for tree-like networks, it often works well on networks containing loops. The paper seeks to explain what its solutions represent in this broader setting and to use that explanation to build better algorithms.

The authors show that if belief propagation converges, its solution must be a stationary point of the approximate Bethe free energy. This characterizes its fixed points through a variational perspective; it does not establish that convergence always occurs. The connection also makes more accurate free-energy approximations from statistical physics available as a basis for extending the algorithm.

Using Kikuchi approximations, the authors derive generalized belief propagation methods. These methods can improve accuracy at an adjustable increase in computational complexity. An example on a grid Markov network produces much more accurate marginal probabilities than ordinary belief propagation. The contribution combines an explanation of existing message-passing solutions with a systematic route to richer approximations.
neurips-2000-generalized-belief-propagat.tldr: Connecting belief propagation fixed points to approximate free energy yields generalized message-passing methods that can trade additional computation for greater accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper presents evidence that several complex statistical properties of natural images and signals can arise from a comparatively simple process. The proposed model changes the scale of an otherwise stationary Gaussian process. These scale changes introduce non-stationarity, allowing the signal's statistical behavior to vary rather than remain fixed.

One consequence is a common description of different natural signals through spherically invariant random processes. For this model family, the joint probability densities can be constructed from a one-dimensional marginal density. This connects the behavior of multiple signal components to a simpler distributional description and provides a shared framework for signals that exhibit the relevant properties.

A second consequence concerns finding useful linear components. In some cases, exploiting non-stationarity with second-order methods produces a basis equivalent to independent components obtained through higher-order methods. The authors demonstrate this on speech components spanning spectral and temporal structure. The finding shows that changing signal statistics can sometimes supply information otherwise extracted using higher-order statistical analysis.
neurips-2000-higher-order-statistical-pr.tldr: Varying the scale of a Gaussian process can explain several natural-signal statistics and sometimes enable second-order recovery of independent-component-equivalent bases.

paragraphs: The paper models memory consolidation: the process through which declarative memories initially dependent on the hippocampus for recall become accessible without it. The authors aim to give a quantitative account of a process that had received extensive experimental and qualitative modeling attention but comparatively little quantitative exploration.

In the model, hierarchical cortical connections initially encode semantic information learned through probabilistic unsupervised learning. During consolidation, these connections also come to encode episodic information. This gives the same cortical hierarchy a changing role, extending what it represents as memories become established.

The hippocampus contributes both to current recall and to the development of later cortical recall. Before consolidation is complete, it helps reconstruct full patterns from partial inputs. It also trains the cortex to perform the appropriate reconstruction independently. The proposed mechanism therefore connects the immediate usefulness of hippocampal pattern completion to the gradual emergence of cortical self-sufficiency. It offers a computational account of how dependence on the hippocampus could diminish as cortical representations change.
neurips-2000-hippocampally-dependent-con.tldr: A hierarchical cortical model explains consolidation through hippocampal pattern completion that also trains the cortex to recall memories independently.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification settings with few labeled examples and additional unlabeled data. It proposes a tractable way for both kinds of examples to contribute to the classifier. The central operation expands each input into a longer feature vector using information from labeled and unlabeled examples.

This feature expansion gives unlabeled data a role in the representation used for discriminative classification. The resulting method can be interpreted as a discriminative kernel density estimate. The authors train it using an expectation-maximization algorithm that, for this formulation, is discriminative and reaches the optimal solution. That optimality claim concerns the proposed estimation problem.

The paper also develops a purely discriminative formulation through the maximum-entropy framework. These two perspectives describe how the expanded representation supports estimation and training. The authors demonstrate high classification accuracy with very few labeled examples. The contribution is thus a specific mechanism for exploiting unlabeled examples, paired with tractable optimization and evidence that the resulting classifier can work with limited labeled data.
neurips-2000-kernel-expansions-with-unla.tldr: Expanding features with labeled and unlabeled examples yields a tractable discriminative classifier demonstrated to achieve high accuracy with few labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a linear transformation of classifier features to reduce the probability of misclassification. The transformation maps an original feature vector into a space of equal or lower dimension. The design objective is minimum Bayes error, tying the representation directly to the classification problem.

The authors explore two criteria for selecting this transformation. One maximizes an average divergence between class densities after projection, favoring separation between classes. The other minimizes a union Bhattacharyya bound in the projected space, using an error bound to guide the representation. Both provide ways to choose features according to their relationship with classification error.

The two approaches perform similarly in practice and outperform standard linear discriminant analysis features in the reported evaluation. On a large-vocabulary telephony speech-recognition task, they yield a 10% relative improvement in word error rate over state-of-the-art cepstral features. This result supports selecting projected speech features through class-separation or error-bound criteria; the reported percentage is a relative improvement, not a percentage-point reduction.
neurips-2000-minimum-bayes-error-feature.tldr: Two error-oriented linear feature-selection methods achieve a 10% relative word-error-rate improvement over cepstral features on a telephony speech task.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the relationship between model complexity and goodness of fit in learning problems. Its focus is the pattern of improvement as a model becomes more complex. The authors study when this relationship has a diminishing-returns character, so that adding complexity brings progressively smaller gains in fit.

The theoretical contribution is to characterize a general class of learning problems for which the goodness-of-fit function has a first-order convexity property as a function of complexity. This gives a mathematical description of the trade-off within that class. The claim concerns problems satisfying the characterization, rather than every possible learning task or model family.

The paper illustrates the property using several real datasets and learning problems, including finite mixture modeling and multivariate linear regression. These examples show the same broad question arising in different settings: how much additional fit accompanies additional complexity? The contribution is a shared account of that relationship, helping explain why increasingly elaborate models can deliver diminishing improvements in the fit being measured.
neurips-2000-model-complexity-goodness-o.tldr: The paper characterizes a class of learning problems with diminishing returns in goodness of fit as model complexity increases.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a computational account of how brain systems support spatial navigation, scene recall, and mental imagery. In the model, the hippocampus stores long-term representations. These are associated with local spatial and object-related features in the parahippocampal region, linking remembered environments with their constituent features.

The parietal portion of the model dynamically constructs representations centered on the viewer from long-term memory. This allows the system to simulate recalling and imagining locations and objects in complex environments. A central mechanism is therefore the generation of a current imagined viewpoint from stored information about a scene.

When the parietal component is damaged, the model shows neglect of one side of imagined space. The neglected side rotates with the observer's imagined perspective, matching the behavior described for the Milan Square experiment. The model also generates predictions about parahippocampal and parietal neural representations and about behavior in healthy people and neuropsychological patients. These predictions extend the proposed mechanism beyond its simulation of the established imagery phenomenon.
neurips-2000-modelling-spatial-recall-me.tldr: A spatial-memory model generates viewer-centered imagery and reproduces perspective-dependent imagined neglect after damage to its parietal component.

paragraphs: The paper examines how quickly neural coding adapts when the statistical properties of a rapidly varying stimulus change. Adaptation allows many neural systems to operate across a wider dynamic range. The authors study its timing in the fly visual system using rapidly varying stimuli whose statistical ensemble is dynamically modulated.

They demonstrate that adaptation to this ensemble dynamically maximizes information transmission about the time-dependent stimulus. This relates adaptation to the information carried by neural responses, giving it a functional interpretation. The relevant question is how the coding of a changing stimulus adjusts as the stimulus statistics themselves change.

The authors also distinguish the timing of adaptation from the timing visible in the firing-rate response. Although that rate response has long transients, adaptation occurs on timescales consistent with optimal estimation of stimulus variance. Thus, a slowly settling rate response does not by itself describe how rapidly the code adjusts. The findings connect multiple response timescales to information transmission and statistical estimation in the examined visual system.
neurips-2000-multiple-timescales-of-adap.tldr: Fly visual adaptation dynamically maximizes transmitted information on timescales consistent with optimal variance estimation, despite long firing-rate transients.

paragraphs: Many statistical learning computations appear to require comparing every data point with every other point. The straightforward approach uses a number of distance calculations proportional to the square of the dataset size, which can become infeasible. The paper develops geometric algorithms for this shared computational structure across six examples.

The examples include nearest-neighbor classification, kernel density estimation, outlier detection, and two-point correlation. The authors present techniques applicable in principle to other N-body-style computations, including those arising in Gaussian mixtures, radial basis function networks, and hidden Markov models. This groups several learning problems around a common computational challenge.

The algorithms have favorable asymptotic scaling and are empirically several orders of magnitude faster than naive computation, even on small datasets. The authors report knowing no more efficient exact algorithms for these problems, either theoretically or empirically. Their framework also extends to more difficult correlation computations, illustrated by multiple two-point correlation and n-point correlation. The contribution combines speed improvements with a broader geometric framework for related computations.
neurips-2000-n-body-problems-in-statisti.tldr: Geometric algorithms accelerate all-pairs statistical learning computations by several orders of magnitude in experiments and extend to harder correlation problems.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic framework for assigning semantic labels to video content. Its basic units, called multijects, connect low-level media features with higher-level concepts. A network of these units, called a multinet, represents contextual relationships among concepts both within a frame and across frames.

The main technical contribution is modeling this network as a factor graph. The relationships include which concepts occur together and how concepts depend on one another over time within a video shot. This makes scene context part of the inference process, allowing evidence about one concept to affect the interpretation of another.

The authors use the sum-product algorithm for exact or approximate inference in these networks. High-level constraints are used to try to correct mistakes made when concepts are detected separately. They report a significant improvement in overall detection performance. The result supports the value of combining individual concept detections with learned spatial and temporal context when producing semantic descriptions for video indexing.
neurips-2000-probabilistic-semantic-vide.tldr: Factor graphs combine concept detections with within-frame and temporal context, significantly improving overall semantic video detection performance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the limitations that large datasets impose on Gaussian process models. It proposes a sparse representation in which a relevant subsample of the data fully specifies the model's predictions. The aim is to retain a compact predictive representation while making Gaussian process modeling more practical as data volume grows.

The method combines a Bayesian online algorithm with sequential construction of that subsample. These are complementary parts of the approach: learning proceeds online, while the data representation is built sequentially around relevant examples. The selected subset serves as the information needed to determine predictions for the resulting model.

Experiments on both toy problems and large real-world datasets indicate that the approach is efficient. These results support combining online Bayesian learning with selective data retention as a way to address large-data limitations. The central contribution is the connection between the learning procedure and the sparse representation: selecting the predictive subsample is integrated into the process of constructing the Gaussian process model.
neurips-2000-sparse-representation-for-g.tldr: Online Bayesian learning and sequential subsample selection produce a sparse Gaussian process representation with empirical evidence of efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a common probabilistic framework for removing noise and reverberation from speech. It formulates both problems as Bayes-optimal signal estimation. The central idea is to use a strong model of speech, trained beforehand on a large collection of clean recordings, to support recovery of speech from degraded observations.

The clean-speech model supplies learned information about the signal being estimated. The framework covers recordings from either a single microphone or multiple microphones. This places the two kinds of degradation and both recording configurations within one estimation approach, with the speech model playing a central role throughout.

To make computation efficient, the authors combine variational expectation-maximization, frequency-domain processing, and conjugate priors. These choices provide the computational machinery for applying the probabilistic formulation. Tests on noisy, reverberant speech produce results substantially better than standard methods. The findings support the use of a pretrained speech model within a unified estimation framework for these combined audio-restoration problems.
neurips-2000-speech-denoising-and-dereve.tldr: A pretrained clean-speech model supports unified Bayesian denoising and dereverberation, with substantially better reported results than standard methods.

paragraphs: The paper asks how people learn simple causal relationships from observed data. It uses graphical models to separate two aspects of this learning problem: estimating the properties of relationships within a given causal structure and determining what the structure itself should be. That distinction frames the authors' account of causal induction.

The authors interpret two leading psychological theories as estimating parameters within a fixed graph. In such an account, learning adjusts a model whose pattern of connections is already specified. They argue that a complete explanation must also address how people learn the underlying causal graph, including which relationships belong in it.

They propose treating this structural learning as Bayesian inference, so that data inform beliefs about possible causal structures. Discussion of three datasets supports their argument. The contribution is a broader account of what causal learning involves: the learner may need to infer the organization of causal relationships as well as their parameters. The paper presents Bayesian structure inference as a model of that additional inductive process.
neurips-2000-structure-learning-in-human.tldr: The paper models human causal induction as Bayesian learning of graph structure as well as estimation of relationships within a graph.

paragraphs: The paper describes a system for extracting diagnostic information from vibrations measured at a jet engine's casing. Its focus is the shape of a vibration signature. The system uses support vector machines for novelty detection, learning a representation of normal behavior against which a signature's unusualness can be assessed.

This framing turns vibration analysis into a comparison with learned normality. The output provides a measure of how unusual the observed shape is, making the representation of normal signatures central to the diagnostic approach. The method therefore connects the statistical characterization of vibration data with the practical task of identifying departures from normal patterns.

The authors also introduce a method for incorporating information from a second class into support vector novelty detection. This extends the information available when constructing the novelty detector. They report results from applying the system to jet-engine vibration analysis. The contribution combines an application-specific diagnostic system with a methodological extension for using second-class information in a normality-based detection framework.
neurips-2000-support-vector-novelty-dete.tldr: Support vector novelty detection measures unusual jet-engine vibration signatures, with a proposed method for incorporating information from a second class.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a way to compare text documents through ordered character subsequences of a fixed length. Characters in a subsequence need not be adjacent, but they must retain their order in the text. This defines a feature space in which document similarity depends on shared character patterns.

Occurrences receive exponentially decreasing weights according to the full span they occupy in the text. Patterns whose characters are close together therefore receive more emphasis than widely separated occurrences. The document kernel is the inner product in this feature space. However, explicitly constructing all features would be prohibitively expensive because the number of possible subsequences grows exponentially with their length.

The authors show how dynamic programming can evaluate the inner product efficiently without constructing the full feature vector. This makes the large implicit representation usable for document comparison. A preliminary classification comparison with a standard word-feature kernel gives encouraging results. The contribution combines a character-sequence notion of similarity with an efficient computation that makes it practical to investigate.
neurips-2000-text-classification-using-s.tldr: A dynamically computed string kernel compares documents through weighted character subsequences, with encouraging preliminary classification results.

paragraphs: The paper develops a counterpart to the kernel trick for algorithms organized around distances. Its goal is to let such algorithms operate in feature spaces that are usually related nonlinearly to the original input space. This provides a way to change the geometry used by a distance-based method.

The key step is identifying a class of kernels that can be represented as distances derived from norms in Hilbert spaces. This representation connects kernel computations with a distance interpretation. It gives the proposed generalization a mathematical basis: the relevant kernels correspond to distances in an appropriate feature space.

The authors further show that familiar kernel methods, including support vector machines and kernel principal component analysis, can themselves be understood as distance-based algorithms and used with this kernel class. The contribution therefore serves two purposes. It extends the kinds of feature-space computations available to distance methods, and it offers a different interpretation of established kernel algorithms that could support the design of new ones.
neurips-2000-the-kernel-trick-for-distan.tldr: A class of distance-representable kernels extends distance-based algorithms to feature spaces and provides a distance interpretation of familiar kernel methods.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much neural coding is shared across individuals and how much differs. Neural coding concerns the relationship between sequences of spikes and the information they convey. The authors formulate the comparison quantitatively using information theory and apply it to experiments in the fly visual system.

They find significant differences between individuals in the structure of the code. These differences are especially evident in how temporal spike patterns convey information beyond what is available from changes in spike rate. The result distinguishes the detailed timing-based organization of a code from a description based only on how often spikes occur.

At the same time, all flies in the studied ensemble show high coding efficiency, with the same amount of information per spike across individuals. Thus, differences in the structure of the code coexist with a shared efficiency measure. The contribution makes individuality and universality separately measurable: individuals can use temporal patterns differently while achieving the same information carried per spike in this ensemble.
neurips-2000-universality-and-individual.tldr: Flies differ in their temporal spike coding while sharing high coding efficiency and the same information per spike in the studied ensemble.
